Only Begotten (Doctrinal)
OHN-lee bih-GOT-uhn
noun
Greek monogenēs (G3439) — "only begotten" or "unique, one-of-a-kind"; the Johannine title of Christ as the unique Son of God (John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18; 1 John 4:9), distinguishing His Sonship from believers' adoptive sonship.

Biblical Definition

Only Begotten is the unique Johannine title for Christ as the sole eternal Son of the Father — the Sonship that distinguishes Christ from believers, who are sons of God by ADOPTION (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:5) and not by eternal generation. The Greek monogenēs appears nine times in the NT, five of them in Johannine writings about Christ: "the only begotten of the Father" (John 1:14); "the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father" (John 1:18); "his only begotten Son" (John 3:16); "the only begotten Son of God" (John 3:18); "his only begotten Son into the world" (1 John 4:9). The word combines monos (only, unique) and genēs (kind, type) — "only of His kind, unique." Older scholarship sometimes read monogenēs as derived from gennaō (to beget) and translated "only begotten" — emphasizing eternal generation. Modern scholarship often prefers "unique, one-of-a-kind" — emphasizing categorical singularity. The Nicene Creed's affirmation "begotten of His Father before all worlds...begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father" preserves the eternal-generation theology against Arian readings (Christ as creature). Whether translated "only begotten" or "unique," the doctrine is the same: Christ is the Son of God in a way that NO ONE ELSE is. Believers' sonship is adoptive (Gal 4:4-5 — God sent forth His Son to redeem...that we might receive the adoption); Christ's Sonship is eternal, essential, ontological. The doctrine guards against modalism (Father and Son as same Person — impossible if Christ is "of" the Father), against Arianism (Christ as created — impossible if Christ is "only begotten" of God's own essence), and against universal-fatherhood theology that flattens distinctions (Christ's Sonship is UNIQUE).

Webster 1828 Definition

Christ as the sole eternal Son of the Father by ontological generation; distinguishes His Sonship from believers' adoptive sonship.

ONLY BEGOTTEN, noun. The unique Johannine title of Christ as the sole eternal Son of the Father. Greek monogenēs.

Five Johannine occurrences referring to Christ: John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18; 1 John 4:9. Distinguishes Christ's Sonship (eternal, essential) from believers' adoptive sonship (received in time, by grace).

Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

John 3:16 — "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

1 John 4:9 — "In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him."

John 1:18 — "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him."

Modern Corruption

Only Begotten is corrupted when modern "universal fatherhood" theology flattens Christ's unique Sonship into one example of universal divine sonship, or when Arianism (modern: Jehovah's Witnesses) reads "begotten" as evidence of Christ being created.

expand to see more

Universal-fatherhood flattening. Modern liberal theology often teaches "the universal fatherhood of God and the universal brotherhood of man" — God is Father to all, Jesus is brother to all equally. But the canonical text is specific: Jesus is the ONLY BEGOTTEN — UNIQUE. We become children of God by ADOPTION through faith in Christ (John 1:12; Gal 4:5); we are not children of God by virtue of being human. The fatherhood of God is COVENANTAL (to His people through Christ), not universal (to humanity in general). To flatten Christ's unique Sonship into universal sonship is to dissolve the gospel's particularity.

Arian "begotten = created" reading. Jehovah's Witnesses argue that "begotten" implies creation in time — "a begotten son is younger than his father." But the Nicene Creed (AD 325) directly answered this: "begotten, not made." Eternal generation means the Son derives His Person from the Father eternally, without ever beginning to exist. The Son is FROM the Father (relation), not made BY the Father (creation). The eternal-generation language preserves both Christ's coequality with the Father and the distinction of Persons. Without it, Trinity collapses.
